1. In the sentence "1. Restructure the line," even a human can't understand what element 'line' refers to. I'm not sure whether the direction of the responses so far is appropriate, but from a designer's perspective 'line' would suggest a line element like a divider, so I first had doubts about the prompt itself.

2. What I thought was a problem from the original design is that there's only one progress bar but two different metrics being shown. So it's unclear whether that progress bar refers to steps or to reviewed cards — I think it actually needed to be fixed down to a single metric.

3. In variant A, the two metrics increased to three, which makes the original design's problem worse. If the planning intent is that all three pieces of info must be shown, I think it would have been more appropriate to just remove the progress bar element. In this variant, the progress bar seems to have no reason to exist.

The designer should have looked at references like 'Speak' or 'Duolingo' sufficiently before writing the prompt. Just looking at a few of those reference screens would immediately show that the current progress bar information layout is inappropriate.

Regarding the request to change the progress bar color, it appropriately picked a highly saturated color that stands out well against a dark background. I also think choosing a green palette that gives a sense of progress rather than a warning-like red palette was appropriate.
The quality got worse to the point that even a layperson who doesn't know much about design would think the overall design became complicated and hard to take in at a glance.

In UX/UI design, yellow mainly means 'caution, warning,' so given that I understood this card as showing 'the user's learning progress,' I doubted whether it's an appropriate color. If the emotion a user would feel from a green progress bar is 'progress, achievement,' the emotion a user would feel from this variant would probably be 'anxiety, unease.' I think it's a color choice that doesn't properly reflect the planning intent.

In particular, the 7-day readiness that used to be at the bottom wasn't moved elsewhere but deleted entirely, so it's closer to removing information than reordering.

Under Health areas, Sleep, Heart & recovery, and Activity are set up as independent cards with related figures and statuses placed together. Unlike the original where information was scattered across Today, Key vitals, and 7-day readiness, it's easy to check status by specific health area. However, the weekly Readiness trend is a composite metric that reflects both sleep and heart rate info, yet it's placed only inside the Heart & recovery card, so the classification's meaning is somewhat ambiguous.

Restructured the original's score-first layout into the order of Balanced recovery description, Sleep and Resting heart rate influencing factors, then Readiness score. Instead of showing the number 82 first, it lets you understand the meaning and basis of the current state first, so the reordering of information leads to a real UX improvement.

After looking at this design, I was reminded of the GenUI interface I'm using to respond to this set right now. What the two UI interfaces have in common is that they try to deliver more information than necessary to the user all at once. Users have a limit on how much information they can process at each step, but neither interface acknowledges this at all — if there's information about steps 1 through 5, they dump all of it on you starting from the first step.

There's a UX/UI law that the person who designed the GenUI interface and the researchers in this study absolutely must check: "Hick's Law." According to Hick's Law, "to reduce cognitive load, break complex tasks into smaller pieces, and when decision time is heavily affected by reaction time, minimize the number of options." I've gotten the impression that the GenUI interface and all the desktop-version designs shown in these sets so far give no consideration whatsoever to that law.

On top of that, I've felt all along that, paradoxically, an interface designed by people who research UX/UI is a design that gives no thought to UX/UI at all. There's a UT site called 'Maze' with a similar task-progression format to GenUI, and if you look at that UT tool, you can see that whenever it explains a task to the user, each screen focuses on just one goal. And when it explains things, it doesn't demand 'explanation / task completion / summarizing results' all at once; it shows them step by step, providing an appropriate amount of information as you move to 'next.' By contrast, the current variant A and the GenUI interface seem to have far too many design choices that induce information overload.
